In 2016, ecologist Kristen Cecala and a workmate saw black-bellied salamanders from Appalachian streams quickly jump at each other in a special box in the lab.
The experiment was set up to test how rising temperatures would affect salamanders’ behavior.
As it turned out, they were nearly four times as likely to act aggressively(好斗) at 25° Celsius, much warmer than their stream habitats.
As the planet warms due to climate change, rising temperatures could affect some species’ social structures and ecosystems.
One possible explanation for this heat-aggression link in cold-blooded animals is that warmth dials up the animals’ metabolisms(代谢), using up more of their energy.
By contrast, warm-blooded animals may be less sensitive to these effects because they can cool their bodies through sweating.
There is indeed some evidence that heat can affect brain chemistry and connectivity, potentially leading to aggressive behavior, says environmental neuroscientist Kim Meidenbauer.
